benjamin-pugh-brooklyn-1900-08-23.A1:
NEGRO SHOT WAITER DEAD Killed White Man Who Served Him in Restaurant.
John Pietden, a waiter, thirty-five years old, of 1400 Gates avenue. Brooklyn, was shot and instantly killed at 2 o'clock this afternoon, by Benjamin Puglis, colored, of 672 Gates avenue.

Puglis was being served in the restaurant where Pietden was employed, at 1719 Fulton street. He expressed dissatisfaction with the service and he and the waiter became involved in a dispute. Suddenly Puglis arose from his seat, and, drawing a revolver from his pocket, fired once at Pietden. Pietden died almost immediately.

The murderer ran out of the restaurant, but was captured after a short pursuit by Policeman Robert Summerville.

There were numerous witnesses of the crime.
benjamin-pugh-brooklyn-1900-08-23.A2:
NEGRO KILLS A WAITER.
WHITE MAN HAD KICKED HIM IN DISPUTE OVER PAYMENT.
CROWD THREATEN TO LYNCH ASSAILANT
—POLICEMAN DRAWS A REVOLVER
TO KEEP IT BACK.
Quarrelling over the failure to pay 10 cents for a dish of corned beef and cabbage, John Tietjen, a white waiter, was shot dead by Benjamin Pugh, a negro patron, in a cheap restaurant at No. 1,719 Fulton-st., Brooklyn, yesterday afternoon. The murder appeared to be premeditated. After the clash over the bill the negro surilily threw down 10 cents on the floor, and defied the white waiter, who responded with several vicious kicks. The negro sought the street, looked for a policeman, and, unable to find one, bought .32-calibre revolver at a hardware store. He returned and shot the waiter.

The four shots fired attracted a small crowd, but the negro escaped through the throng to a nearby house in Marion-st., where he was placed under arrest. He was locked up in the Schenectady-ave police station. Though a crowd of about three hundred gathered during the arrest, there was no concerted attempt to harm the prisoner, though there were cries of "Lynch him!" Lynch him!" A policeman drew a revolver and threatened the crowd, which fell back.

WAITER'S MANNER HAUGHTY.

It was a little after 1 o'clock yesterday afternoon that the negro, who has been employed as a waiter on the Stonington Line steamboat Providence, entered the restaurant. He took a seat at one of the side tables. He was the only negro in the restaurant. The white waiter, John Tietjen, came up to him reluctantly.

"Well, what's your order?" asked Tietjen, in a haughty manner, as though his pride had been pricked at having to wait on a man with a black skin.

"Cornedbeef and cabbage," replied the negro, glancing up at the waiter. They exchanged challenging looks.

After eating the food the negro pushed back his chair, arose and started for the door.

"None of that!" shouted Tietjen. "Pay your money, or it's up with you."

The negro stopped, grinned, and finally feeling in one of his trousers' pockets for coin, fished out two nickels.
SPRINGS AT THE NEGRO.

The waiter boiled with rage. He sprang at the negro and gave him several kicks. The negro went across the street to a saloon. He asked for a policeman. None were about. He disappeared down the street. He entered the hardware store of Andrew Gilroy, at No. 1,744 Fulton-st., and said he wanted to get a revolver. He finally selected a .32-calibre bulldog revolver, paying $1.68 for the weapon.

He returned to the open door of the restaurant. Tietjen saw him, but he was busy at the moment making change for a customer.

"Come out heah and fight," called the negro, following this with a number of vile names, the spectators say.

"I'll be with you on the spot," answered the waiter, returning the negro's expletives with venom.

The men met at the doorway. There were a few preliminary jabs and attempted thrusts at each other's bodies, when the negro pulled from his hip pocket the revolver, aiming it at Tietjen, who was only a foot or two away. He pulled the trigger four times.

The first bullet hit Tietjen over the heart, and he fell to the floor. The second bullet entered the brain of the fallen man, just over the right ear. The two following bullets went wild. Tietjen died instantly.

TRIES TO MAKE HIS ESCAPE.

As soon as Pugh saw his enemy was dead he thrust the revolver back into his pocket and started away. Fireman J. Keenan saw the man fire the last shot as he was riding by in a trolley car. He leaped from the car and made for the negro, who, seeing a pursuer, ran down the street into Marion-st and into the house at No. 20, with Keenan and a dozen other men in pursuit. With a bound Pugh reached the second floor, and then, turning on Keenan, defied him to touch him.
into Marion-st and into the house at No. 20, with Keenan and a dozen other men in pursuit. With a bound Pugh reached the second floor, and then, turning on Keenan, defied him to touch him. Keenan, not a whit afraid, rushed for the negro, and they closed in a fierce struggle. While they were grappling Policeman Summergill and a street sweeper arrived. The policeman subdued the negro and placed him under arrest.

Half a dozen other policemen and a small crowd had in the mean time arrived. The crowd was threatening, but kept back when ordered to do so.

The sergeant at the station said that the negro admitted doing the shooting, and added:

"I will die in the electric chair. I am perfectly willing to do so."

Detective McCurdy, of the Schenectady-ave, police station, found the revolver in the Marion-st house, where the negro had lost it in the struggle. Mr. Gilroy went to the police station, and, according to the sergeant, identified the negro as the man who had bought the revolver a little after 1 o'clock.
benjamin-pugh-brooklyn-1900-08-23.A3:
NEGRO MURDERS A WAITER. SHOOTS HIM TWICE AFTER BEING FORCED TO PAY HIS BILL.
Bought a Revolver and Then Went Back and Invited the Walter Out to Fight—Captured After a Chase by a Fireman He Threatened to Stab—Demonstration by the Crowd.

Benjamin Pugh, a negro, 25 years old, of 672 Gates avenue, Brooklyn, shot and killed John Tietjen, a waiter, of 1400 Gates avenue, in Charles Hoffman's restaurant at 1719 Fulton street, at 2 o'clock yesterday afternoon. Pugh, who is a porter employed by the Stonington Steamboat Company, entered the restaurant shortly after 1 o'clock and called for corned beef hash. He was served, but found fault with the way the hash was cooked. After eating it, he started to leave the restaurant without paying for the meal. Tietjen ran after him and forced him back to the counter. The negro then put two five-cent pieces on the counter. As Tietjen was about to pick up the money the negro brushed the two coins off the counter. They fell on the floor.

"If you want the money, there it is," said the negro to Tietjen.

"I wouldn't allow a white man to treat me that way," said Tietjen, who made the negro pick the coins from the floor.

Then Tietjen hustled him out of the restaurant. Pugh went across Fulton street to a saloon, where he had several drinks. From there he went to the store of Andrew Gilroy at 1744 Fulton street, and purchased a revolver of the "Young America" design, paying $1.90 for it. He also purchased five cents' worth of cartridges and then left.

It was about 2 o'clock when Pugh returned to the restaurant. He stood in front of the door and challenged Tietjen to fight it out.

Tietjen started from behind the counter a just as he was turning toward the door. Pugh fired four shots. One of them struck Tietjen in the left side of the head, another pierced his breast and the other two were lodged in the wall of the restaurant. Tietjen fell to the floor, dead. The negro then ran up Fulton street and into Marion street.

He was followed by William Cooper of 121 Hull street, who is employed in the restaurant as a cook: Frank Walsh of 15 Bancroft place, Lem Caskey of 97 Sumpter street, all of whom witnessed the shooting, and Fireman Peter J. Keenan of Engine Company No. 127, who was on a Fulton street car. Keenan saw the negro running with a revolver in his hand. He jumped off the car and gave chase. Pugh ran into the house at 20 Marion street near Reid avenue. Keenan followed him to the first floor, when Pugh pulled a knife from his pocket and threatened to kill him. The fireman stepped aside and Pugh attempted to run down stairs. Keenan tripped him up and the murderer fell down the stairs. Keenan then grabbed him and held him until Policeman Summergill of the Atlantic avenue station arrived. By this time a large crowd had gathered. Word was sent to the police station and the patrol wagon with six patrolmen were sent to the scene.

When the crowd saw the negro being brought from the barn, there were cries of "Lynch him!" "Lynch the nigger!" He was trembling with fear but was taken to the station without meeting with any violence. He acknowledged to Detective McCurdy that he had shot Tietjen and said he did so because Tietjen had assaulted him. When he was told that Tietjen was dead he said:

"I suppose I'll go to the electric chair, but I don't care. He assaulted me and I only protected myself."

Tietjen lived with his wife and four children. His body was taken home last evening. Tietjen had the reputation of being of a quiet disposition. The witnesses say that he made no attempt to assault Pugh, but that he was probably intending to go out into the street and call a policeman when Pugh fired the shots that killed him. The police recovered the revolver in the hallway of the Marion street house.
benjamin-pugh-brooklyn-1900-08-23.A5:
KILLED THE WAITER.
Impatient Negro Shoots Attendant in Restaurant.
New York, Aug. 23.—John Tietgen, a waiter in a Brooklyn restaurant, was shot and instantly killed to-day by Benjamin Puglis, a colored man.

Puglis ordered a lunch, which, not being served quickly enough to suit him, caused him to enter into an altercation with the waiter. During the quarrel the negro drew a pistol and shot the waiter in the breast, killing him instantly. The murderer made no attempt to escape and was locked up by a policeman who was summoned.
benjamin-pugh-brooklyn-1900-08-23.A7:
PUGH CALLS IT SELF-DEFENCE.
ENTERS PLEA OF NOT GUILTY AGAINST CHARGE
OF MURDER.
Benjamin Pugh, the negro who shot and instantly killed John Tietjen, a white waiter, in the restaurant at No. 1,710 Fulton-st., Brooklyn, on Thursday in a quarrel over the payment for an order, was arraigned yesterday on a charge of murder in the first degree before Magistrate Teale, in the Gates-ave, police court. When Pugh arrived at the police court a crowd, which had collected outside of the building, hooted at him. His lawyer entered a plea of not guilty, and Magistrate Teale set the examination for this morning. Pugh was then taken to the Raymond Street Jail. As he was going out of the court some one asked him why he committed the murder, and it is alleged that he replied: "I thought a colored man had as much right to defend himself as a white man."
benjamin-pugh-brooklyn-1900-08-23.A8:
SATURDAY, AUGUST 25, 1900.
TWO STORIES FROM NEW YORK
We find in the New York Tribune of yesterday a story which interests us no little, in view of the fact that the incident followed so closely upon the recent race riots in that city.

A negro went into a cheap restaurant and took a seat at a table. He was the only negro in the restaurant and John Tietjen, a white waiter, went up to take his order. As soon as the white waiter saw the negro, his blood was up, and the Tribune tells us that he assumed a haughty manner towards his patron in black. Here was the beginning of the trouble. The white man resented the idea of serving a black man, the black man saw it and there was enmity between these two from the start. However, business is business. The negro gave his order and the white man executed it. Finally when the negro had finished eating he started out without paying his score. The white waiter stopped him and demanded the money. The negro took two nickels out of his pocket and threw them at the white man in an insolent manner, telling him to "pick 'em up." The white man needed no further challenge. He at once sprang upon the negro and kicked him out of the door.

The negro then went out and secured a pistol, and everybody knows that when you get a negro and a gun in combination you may look out for trouble. Having armed himself the negro went back to the restaurant and called to the white waiter to come out and fight. The white waiter accepted the challenge and in a little while they were at it tooth and nail. The negro's opportunity had come. He had put that pistol in his pocket for a purpose and when the occasion offered, he pulled it out and shot the white man through the heart.

The negro then ran off to a neighboring house and a large crowd of whites ran after him. The negro was caught and the whites threatened to lynch him, but the officers of the law got the negro safely out of the way and landed him in jail.

From the same paper, and it must be remembered that the Tribune is the National Republican organ, we clip another interesting story, as follows.

What threatened to be a serious trouble in the Warlow Athletic Club, of Whitestone, has been averted. The trouble started over the admittance of Arthur Rhodes, a negro, to membership. The club has an Investigating Committee, which is supposed to pass on all persons proposed for membership, but it made no investigation when Rhodes' name was proposed by William Knabe.

A few nights ago the club voted to admit those who had been proposed and posted for membership. It was not until a day or two later that it became known generally to the members that Rhodes was a negro. Some favored allowing him to rehain, as he was known as a young man of good habits, but others objected to remaining in the club with him. Last evening the affair was settled by a letter of resignation from Rhodes. He said he did not wish to be the cause of any trouble in the club.

These stories show for themselves. They show that the people of the North are face to face with the negro question and they are fast finding out what it means.
benjamin-pugh-brooklyn-1900-08-23.A9:
BOROUGH ITEMS.
The Long Island Railroad siding to the Long Pier, Sag Harbor, will probably be built soon, as Justice Mattice yesterday dismissed the motion for an injunction against the work, made by the Fahys Watch Case Company, of Sag Harbor.

The first work in the construction of a new bridge to replace the old Grand-st. bridge was begun yesterday. The bridge was closed yesterday, and the Grand-st. cars will in the future turn out of Grand-st., into Flushing-ave., and thence to Metropolitan-ave., and across the bridge.

Benjamin Pugh, the negro who shot down John Tietjen, a white waiter in a restaurant at No. 1,719 Fulton-st., last Thursday afternoon, was held for the action of the Grand Jury by Magistrate Teale yesterday.

According to the figures given out by General Manager J. C. Brackenridge yesterday, the Brooklyn Rapid Transit Company carried eight hundred thousand people on its various lines on Sunday. This is the record of the company.

elijah-clark-huntsville-1900-07-23.A1:
A Sensational Lynching.
A very sensational lynching occurred at Huntsville, Ala., on Monday of last week. A mob of one thousand men took Elijah Clark, a negro twenty years old, from the jail, hung him to a tree and riddled his body with bullets. The crime for which he met such condign punishment was that of rape upon the person of a twelve-year-old white girl, that he attacked in a lonely field. A smaller sister that was with the girl ran and gave the alarm, and a large crowd was soon on his heels and a large crowd captured by the Sheriff's deputies and put in jail. A mob gathered and demanded the keys. The Sheriff refused, saying he would die before he would give the prisoner up. The mob then threw a stick of dynamite into the jail, which blew out the front windows and damaged the stairway. The Sheriff's deputies fired on the crowd and a man was wounded in the shoulder. This enraged the mob still more and they built a fire of oil, tar and feathers on the concrete floor of the basement of the jail with the view of smoking the jailer out. Fearing the jailer, who had retreated to the third floor, was smothering, the Chief of Police dashed up the stairs and brought the unwilling officer down. The mob then had things their own way, and breaking the lock of the steel cell, they took the wretched negro to his victim, who at once identified him, and a little while later his lifeless body was swinging in the wind, a ghastly warning to living brutes such as he.
elijah-clark-huntsville-1900-07-23.A3:
A Determined Mob.
Seldom has there been such grave determination on the part of the mob or such dogged resistance on the part of a sheriff as that displayed at Huntsville, Ala., last week. A mob of one thousand men went to the jail to take a negro rapist and lynch him. The Sheriff and his deputies fired upon the lynchers, wounding some of them. This did not deter them. The sheriff appealed to the governor, and the military were ordered out, but too late. The mob received tar and feathers and oil, and having gotten into the lower corridor of the jail, piled them on the casement floor and fired them. The work of smoking out the inmates was begun. The sheriff retreated with his prisoner to a point fartherest removed from the odoriferous pile. He swore that he would die with his prisoner. The chief of police forced his way to where the sheriff was and exhorted him to leave the building. The sheriff was then half suffocated. The official had securely locked his prisoner in a strong cell. The police chief seized the sheriff and dragged him unconscious from the building. The mob took hold of the prisoner and carried him from the jail and hanged and shot him to death.
elijah-clark-huntsville-1900-07-23.A5:
VENGEANCE OF A MOB.
Wreaked on a Brutal Negro at Huntsville, Ala.—Hanged and Filled with Bullets.
Huntsville, Ala., Ju.y 24.—Elijah Clark, a negro who on Sunday assaulted Susan Priest, a 13-year-old girl, was taken from the jail in this city Monday night and lynched near the spot where his crime was committed. His body was riddled with bullets. Sheriff Fulgham defended his prisoner to the last, but a dense smoke, from a combination of tar, feathers and oil, fired by the crazed mob, was too much for him and he was dragged from the jail and placed under a physician's care. William Vining, who attempted to rush through the crowd and up the jail steps, was shot and dangerously wounded.

elijah-clark-huntsville-1900-07-23.A17:
NORTHERN DAILIES ON THE NEW ORLEANS MOB.
It is to be hoped that the authorities of New Orleans will not remain content with the more restoration of order. The crimes committed by this mob are hideous. It has deliberately murdered persons guilty of no offense and in no way related to the original trouble. It has destroyed the property of peaceful citizens. The Police department should ferret out the leaders of this mob and they should be punished as a warning. Meanwhile, the people of New Orleans have been voting millions of money for better water and a more perfect sewerage system and for other municipal improvements. Would it not be well to expend a few thousand dollars for the strengthening of the police force, so that peaceful citizens may be protected from mobs? If life and property are not safe other municipal improvements will be of little account. The thugs of New Orleans are in no respect more civilized or human than the Boxers of China.—The Chicago Tribune. The killing of the negro at New Orleans may have been justified to some extent. He was a desperate character, had slain several policemen and defied arrest. But there was no excuse for the savagery that followed, for it was a relapse into savagery that caused hundreds of people to empty the contents of revolvers and guns into the body of the dead negro as it lay in the street, and it was the barbarity of the heathen that suggested the burning of the remains. The mob in this case was not composed of the scum of the city. Good citizens forming the special posse, soldiers and policemen, were carried away by the excitement—permitted inherent savagery to break forth—and the barbarous exhibition followed. We accuse the Chinese Boxers of being fanatical heathen because, under the influence of excitement, they have mur ered Christians. What should we call those civilized people at home who scour the streets of a city, shooting at every negro that shows his head? Germany is a so-called highly civilized country. What should we call Emperor William, who has instructed his soldiers to give no quarter when they land in China? "Spare nobody," which means that all women and children must be put to the sword, was the Emperor's order. If this be not a relapse into savagery, what is it?—The Indianapolis Journal. The rioting and killing at New Orleans are entirely without palliation. The

ANARCHISTS GLOAT
Over the Assassination of Humbert By One of Their Number. ACT IS APPROVED IN OPEN MEETING "Death to All Monnrchu" Is Shiboleth of the Order at Paterson, New Jersey. There was a meeting of anarchihts in Paterson,N.J., Tuesday night,at which the killing of King Humbort was endorsed. A reporter who sought admittance was welcomed, as it was said that these anarchists wanted the whole world to know their sentiments. The principal speaker at the meeting was Earnest Crevalla, 21 years of age. In the course of an impassioned address he said: "We are members of the group of anarchists to which Bressi belonged. He is a martyr. He has done what we would have had him do. Ask me, do we endorse the killing of King Humbert? I will answer the question before you ask it. Of course we do. It was not our instruction to Bressi to kill, but he has done what he knew to be right, and we will sustain him and give him our sympathy. Was Humbert ever kind to us? No. Was he good to the poor? No. He was a monarch, and all monarchs, according to our vows, must die. "Let Nicholas of Russia tremble, and let the new king of Italy prepare for death. They are both inhuman. They are inhuman because they are monarchs. They would not consent to take the places on the thrones if they were not inhuman. It is a republic that we want, and it is a republic that anarchists in every country will have." Then came an implied threat against high officials in this country, when the young man shouted: "They have run us out of Italy, where to have stayed would have been to starve, and we have come here. An Alabama Mob Gets a Negro Despite Stout Resistance.
HANGED VICTIM FROM A TREE.
Elijah Clark Lynched in the Outskirts of Huntsville — Sheriff Protected Him From a Mob That Threw Dynamite— When Fires Were Set About the Jail the Sheriff Gave In.

Birmingham, Ala. (Special).—A mob of 2000 citizens of Madison County, after an exciting day's effort in surrounding the county jail at Huntsville, Ala., succeeded in getting possession of Elijah Clark, a negro, who had committed an assault on Susie Priest, a thirteen-year-old girl at Dallas, a factory suburb of Huntsville. The negro was taken to the scene of his crime and there strung up, after which the mob dispersed with bitter expressions of hatred for Sheriff Fulgham, who kept them at bay all day long.

When the alarm had been given a posse of citizens went in search of the negro. The search was continued all night, and by daylight two deputy sheriffs overtook Clark and succeeded in getting him in the county jail at Huntsville, a modest, though strong, structure. Word was passed around that the negro was in jail and a mob began forming at once. Five hundred men came from Dallas, and soon a howling mob was around the jail. Meantime Sheriff Fulgham had summoned all his deputy sheriffs and stationed them inside the jail, determined to defend his prisoner. The mob was determined, however, and laid dynamite charges around the jail, intent on blowing it up.

Sheriff Fulgham, in the midst of the excitement, made an address through a window, telling the mob that its members must obey the law, and if they would desist the negro would have a speedy trial. He also announced that Judge Speak, of the Circuit Court, would hold a special term of the court at 3 o'clock in the afternoon, but the mob hooted the sheriff. He then warned them that they must desist. There were a few shots fired at this time. No outbreak occurred, but two men, William Vining and Thomas Johnson, laborers in the cotton factory, were carried off wounded, the first in a dangerous condition.

The mob continued its hooting and informed the sheriff that the jail would be blown up and that he would be killed with the negro. Governor Johnston was notified by wire, but nothing could be done. Troops in and around Huntsville were practically without ammunition, and it would have been useless to call them out.

At noon a piece of dynamite was thrown on the front steps of the jail and exploded with a loud report. Considerable damage was done, but once more Sheriff Fulgham and his deputies kept the crowd at bay.

"Surrender the negro, give him to us," the mob shouted.

Sheriff Fulgham shouted back:

"Stand back, or I'll order my men to fire on you."

Telegrams were received by the Sheriff from United States officials to protect the Federal prisoners in the jail, even if it was necessary to release them. Finally, late in the afternoon, it became noised about that
It took only a few moments to get hold of the negro. He was dragged out and great shout rent the air. The mob half dragged and half pulled the victim along. To Dallas they headed, and once there, to a tree limb the negro was soon dangling.

It was the most exciting day Huntsville ever saw. Women and children trembled in their homes, fearing the outcome Militia in Decatur, Birmingham, Florence and at other points practically rested on their arms, expecting to be called out.

Sunday evening about 6:30 o'clock a deplorable tragedy was enacted as a sequel to a baseball game on the ball grounds near the lake at this place. James Offutt, colored, was shot and killed by Lee Cozart, deputy marshal for Earlington. Offutt was acting as special policeman for that day to keep the peace on the ball grounds during a battle between the colored teams own testiment, didn't and Madisonville. Many witnesses and Him in the full record of the firemony at the examining trial to tell the whole story. We have counted both men among our friends and would not do an injustice to the living nor violence to the memory of the dead.

As the examining trial occupied all of yesterday and a large number of witnesses were heard for both the prosecution and the defense it is impossible to get the full testimony up to the time of going to press.

We have the testimony that was given at the coroner's inquest but that is only a part of the mass of evidence and being unable to give all we deem it wise and just to refrain from publishing any part until all can be heard.

Both men were acting as peace officers. Offutt had suppressed a Madisonville negro who had been flourishing a revolver and had taken the revolver from him. Cozart saw the action, remarked "there is a man with a gun," and started for Offutt. When he reached Offutt, a struggle occurred, Cozart using his billie over Offutt's head, which ended in Cozart shooting Offutt under the chin, the bullet ranging upward causing instant death. Offutt seems to have had the pistol of the Madisonville negro and his own when Cozart came upon him and may have had one of them in his hand. The prosecution claims that Cozart was hasty and the shooting unwarranted and produce evidence that Offutt tried to ward off Cozart's blows and called on him to give him time to explain. The defense claims that Cozart did not know Offutt was acting as an officer, did not know the man he came upon was Offutt, and that Offutt resisted arrest and presented a pistol at Cozart so that the latter thought his life in danger, when he fired. These seem to be perhaps the chief points in the claims of the prosecution

and defense before the mass of testimony at the examining trial has been whipped into shape and digested.

The character and standing of both the principals in this unfortunate affair and all considerations of peace and the execution of even handed justice in the community make it on all accounts of the deepest interest to the entire community.

Lee Cozart is a quite, industrious business man with many friends. He has acted as deputy marshal of Earlington and on many occasions shown himself fearless and capable.

Jim Offutt was a most quiet circumspect colored citizen, intellegent, worthy of utmost confidence and one of the first men of his race in Hopkins county.

The true friends of both men and of the sober, industrious and peacable community in which this tragedy has been enacted desire a careful dispassionate and complete investigation and whatever decision the law demands under the facts. With such investigation and determination every citizen should, and we believe, will be satisfied.

JUDGE HALL'S OPINION. Rendered in Case of the Commonwealth Against Lee Cozart for Killing of James Offutt. MAKES IT ALL A FEARFUL MISTAKE Cozart Discharged After a Rigid Inquiry of Large Number of Witnesses.
Recognizing the great interest of our citizens of town and county in the unfortunate tragedy enacted on the Earlington ball ground on August 19, THE BEE arranged to get a complete report of the case in order to be able to give an intelligent and impartial account. The number of witnesses introduced makes it out of the question to attempt to publish the evidence as brought out in court, but we publish in full the decision of Judge Hall, in which he takes pains to explain his grounds for the conclusion he reaches.

The investigation on the part of the commonwealth, conducted by Judge James Breathitt of Hopkinsville, in a rigid and careful manner and he made a strong argument in favor of the holding of Cozart on the charge of manslaughter. Speeches for the defence were made by Jerrold Jonson and C. J. Waddill.

The opinion of Judge Jno. G. B. Hall is as follows.

Opinion of Judge John G. B. Hall, in case of Commonweaith vs. Lee Cozart.

While the law does not require, that I give the reasons in detail for the conclusions reached by me in the hearing of this trial, the great interest taken and more or less excitement manifested upon the part of the public, and especially the friends of the parties to the tragedy, make it appropriate that I give my reasons.

I, of course, have no interest in this matter other than as a citizen, and an officer striving to do his full duty, and having heard all of the evidence that probably ever can be adduced by diligent friends and able ones, my mind is fully satisfied as to my duty and what I say may have some good effect upon the minds of those who have not investigated so fully.

The colored man, Jim Offutt, who was killed, was proven to be a good citizen, much above the average of his race. He had been sworn in as an officer for that day and while he had not been lawfully appointed, and was not in fact an officer, he thought he was, and in good faith was acting as such.

It is an awful thing to take the life of any human being. Of course it is more serious to take the life of a good citizen than a bad one, but for one to be killed who is acting in good faith as an officer of the law is indeed lamentable.

I believe from the evidence that each party thought he was doing his duty as an officer at the beginning of this trouble. When Offutt went up to that wagon to take a pistol from that Madisonville colored man he was doing his duty as an officer. He had taken this large blue pistol from Perry, and had drawn his own bright, shiny pistol, and was holding it in his hand in that excited crowd when the defendant, Lee Cozart, drove up in his buggy. Cozart sees this conduct and swears that he knew nothing of Offutt having been appointed police and the evidence does not show that he was likely to have known it. He knows there is a difficult up between the Earlington and Madisonville boys. He jumps from his buggy, draws his billy and pistol as he enters the crowd, and he knew this man Offutt was an Earlington man but did not know his name. Offutt does not know that he is coming, and he puts up his own shiny pistol, and sticks this large blue pistol in his hip pocket. A commonwealth witness said he stood behind Offutt and looked at this large blue pistol in his hip pocket. Mr. Cozart comes up to Offutt with pistol and billy in hand. It is insisted that this was wrong. In the quietude of this court room, we might say that an officer should carry the power of law in his face and bearing, and I admit a man is not patriot who does not respect and submit to the man coming in the name of the law, but I doubt that if many of us would give the man whom we seek to arrest, and who, when last seen has his pistol out, so great an advantage in a crowd like that. Mr. Cozart steps up to Offutt, puts his hand on him and just

is no doubt one of these expressions was used, there being no material difference, which many heard and many claim they did not.

The defendant claims that Offutt said "no you don't want to arrest me," or "by God you don't want to arrest me." Many witnesses agree that he said "no by God you don't want me," while others did not hear either say any thing. There is considerable evidence to show that defendant did not know that the colored man was acting as an officer, but the fact that Offutt called the name of Mr. Coil in addressing Mr. Cozart shows that he recognized Cozart as an officer, Mr. Coil being the regular known officer of Earlington. How sad it is that Offutt did not say "I am an officer," if he had, this trouble might have been averted but Offutt raised his hand to or towards his inside vest pocket as if to draw his pistol, and Cozart grabs his hand and strikes him with his club at least twice; some say four or five times during the trouble. Offut has his pistol out and up as if trying to strike or shoot with it. Why he preferred to use his own defective pistol instead of the fine blue revolver of Perry's we can't say, unless he knew his was loaded and he had not examined the blue one. This no one can tell.

Mr. Cozart claims that he saw no police star on Offutt's breast. I wondered at this as the evidence was being given, and the proof plain that a star had been there that afternoon, but this was explained by a statement of one of the last witnesses testifying for the Commonwealth which seems to have been overlooked in the argument. The witness stated that he picked the star up from the ground and pinned it on Offut after he had been killed. Just when this star fell no one can tell.

So we must look at this trouble, and the defendant's conduct from his standpoint, and regard him as arresting a man who was not an officer, but who was resisting an arrest.

It is an unfortunate affair, but one for which the defendant can not be blaimed. There is no reason for any ill will to exist between the colored men of Earlington and Madisonville, or between the white and colored citizens. I make the statement for the future good and you who are interested will do well to heed what I say. I would have no hesitancy whatever in holding this defendant, if I could find that he had abused the power of an officer, or done wrong; but the evidence fully warrants me in acquitting the defendant which I now do.

THE "RED SHIRT" TERROR
OF NORTH CAROLINA.
[BY TELEGRAPH TO THE TRIBUNE.]

Raleigh, N. C., Aug. 1.—Yesterday at a "Red Shirt" meeting in Wilmington Congressman J. D. Bellamy declared that it was the bounden duty of the white men to forcibly expel United States Senator Marion Butler from the State. This opinion was indorsed by A. M. Waddell, Mayor of Wilmington, who followed Bellamy in a "Red Shirt" speech. Tc-day Senator Butler, who is here running the Populist campaign, sent Mr. Bellamy the following letter:

Raleigh, N. C., August 1.
To the Hon. J. D. Bellamy, Wilmington, N. C.
Sir: You are quoted in the Raleigh morning newspapers as saying in a speech at Wilmington yesterday that the Democrats should forcibly expel me from the State. Do you mean that you feel it your duty to forcibly expel me from the State, or do you mean that some one else should do it? Do you mean that one man should undertake it, or that a cowardly, lawless mob should do it? Now, if you think I should be expelled from the State, I suggest that you undertake the job yourself. You are one man and I am one man. If you mean what you say and have any courage (except when you have a mob of "Red Shirts" behind you), I suggest that you proceed to Raleigh and begin the expelling business at once. If you have not the courage to undertake this job, then I suggest that you have the decency to keep your mouth shut. Respectfully,

MARION BUTLER,
Chairman.

It is the terror inspired by such declarations as those of Waddell and Bellamy that has kept Senators Butler and Pritchard out of forty counties in Eastern Carolina. Neither one of these Senators has dared to go east of Raleigh during this campaign; in fact, Senator Pritchard has not been to Raleigh since May 1. Governor Russell had intended to go to Brunswick County to vote, but he has been advised that the condition of the State is such that he ought to remain here, and he has decided to do so.

In order to be in readiness for any emergency, the Governor has now under arms one company of the State Guard here ready to move on nor
It brings the blush to one's cheeks to see how unblushingly and ever approvingly the highhanded abrogation in North Carolina of the common rights of American people is reported in certain papers that ought to represent the higher instincts of the Anglo-Saxon race, for whose supremacy they are doing battle. It matters not that men have spoken untruthfully and bitterly. They have the right to speak. Freedom of speech! Freedom to make political speeches is a cardinal doctrine of our State and Nation. It is a shame upon us that any man has been deprived of his right. It is a shame, too, that bodies of citizens have taken the law into their own hands. To do this is to sow the wind—and the harvest is certain. Let us stop it. If we do not we are lost. We need not listen to those speakers.

The "Red Shirts" are out in force throughout the State. They escort Charles B. Aycock, Democratic candidate for Governor, from place to place, and make great demonstrations for him. The gang from one county does duty in its own county and to the next appointment, and until the gang of the next relieves it. With their blood red shirts, cowboy hats, military leggins, pistols in their belts and Winchester rifles in their arms, galloping horseback over the country, firing off their weapons and shooting skyrockets, they make an appearance not to be forgotten.

They give orders about negroes registering, about attending political speakings, and to stay away from the polls on Election Day. Their duties in this campaign are systematic and thorough. They say the State must be carried on Thursday next for the Democrats by any means that may be required and at any cost. To-day, at Smithfield, Johnston County, a Populist speaker by the name of Teague was taken from the stand and driven out of the town by one thousand "Red Shirts." He committed no offence except that he attempted to speak at an appointment made for him. Several other Populists were shot and cut, and, this being among all white people, the Populists fought, and a number of Democrats were also hurt.

J. D. Parker, chairman of the Republican County Committee and Editor of "The Weekly Courier," was driven into his office by the mob, but his friends prevented the destruction of his office and his death until Governor Russell could be asked for troops. After the troops were ordered out the Sheriff restored order. In Duplin County, on Saturday last, United States District Attorney Bernard prosecuted a Democratic Register, and when Bernard got on the train on his return to Raleigh the "Red Shirts" thrust him on the cars and hooted at him and jeered him, and used all kinds of threatening language, and told him if he came back during the campaign they would hang him. Persons along with Bernard say he would have been killed if the conductor had not interfered and protected him.

H. F. Sewell, Populist candidate for Lieutenant-Governor, had an appointment at Laurinburg, in Robeson County, and was met at the train by five hundred "Red Shirts" and was ordered to remain on the train under pain of death if he got off and attempted to speak. He did not get off, and as the train moved out he

was covered with rotten eggs. In Rockingham County the "Red Shirt" craze has been so great that the Rev. James S: Lawson, a Baptist minister, has entirely lost his mind and has been put in the asylum at Morganton. At the town of Wilson last week an old negro went with his son to register. The official refused to register the son, and the old negro remarked that the register knew more about the age of his son than his father did, whereupon the "Red Shirts" standing around fell upon the two negroes and beat them nearly to death.

Ex-Populist Congressman Fowler had an appointment to speak in the town of Washington, and was met by the "Red Shirts" and assisted on a boat which carried him away from there without speaking. It is openly boasted by the Democrats that by having the "Red Shirts" at the places of registration not less than twenty-five thousand negroes have refused to register. In Scotland County, of one thousand negroes, only twenty-five registered. Oscar J. Spears, Assistant United States Attorney, filled an appointment in Durham last night, and as he left the courthouse the "Red Shirts" threw a bushel of rotten eggs at him, many of them striking his person.

The state is simply a "Red Shirt" camp, and will continue so until the election is over. It is expected that thousands of Republicans and Populists will be challenged on Election Day and prevented from voting. All semblance of a republican form of government has vanished, and the cry is that the end justifies the means.

Ex-Judge W. R. Allen, when in the Legislature, announced that the present Election law was formed for the purpose of securing the adoption of the proposed constitutional amendment, and when that was done an election law would be enacted that would compel an honest election. The scenes of the days of secession are being re-enacted every day. The "Red Shirts" roamed the State then, and after them came the Ku Klux, and the terror is just as widespread as, or more so than, on either of the former occasions. Old citizens say they never expected in a time of profound peace to witness the absence of civil liberty and deprivation of personal liberty and the corruption and debauchery of the ballot that now exist throughout the "old North State."
